content: Paget's disease of the breast is a rare condition characterized by eczematous changes in the skin of the nipple, often associated with an underlying breast malignancy. It was first identified by James Paget in 1874, with earlier descriptions of its clinical features by Velpeau in 1856. The connection between Paget's disease and intraductal carcinoma was established by Jacobeus in 1904, and the epidermotropic theory, which suggests that carcinoma cells from the ducts migrate to the nipple, was supported by Muir and Inglis in the mid-20th century. The first documented case in a male was reported by Elbogen in 1908. Paget's disease accounts for 0.5–5% of all breast cancer cases and is almost always associated with an underlying malignancy, either overt or occult. Over 90% of patients with Paget's disease have an associated breast carcinoma, with 40–45% of these cases linked to ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). The disease is more common in postmenopausal women, typically after the age of 60, but it can also occur in adolescents and the elderly. While it predominantly affects females, males can also develop Paget's disease, though male breast cancer represents less than 1% of all breast cancers, and Paget's disease accounts for only 1–3% of male breast malignancies. Histopathologically, Paget's disease is characterized by the presence of malignant glandular epithelial cells, known as Paget cells, within the epidermis of the nipple. These cells are typically organized in nest-like or gland-like patterns and are preferentially located in the basal layer of the epidermis. Immunohistochemical staining is crucial for diagnosis, with markers such as cytokeratin 7 (CK7), epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), and c-erb-B2 (HER2) being commonly used. Paget cells are strongly associated with Ki-67 and HER2 expression, which helps distinguish them from Toker cells, a normal cell type found in the nipple epidermis. The clinical presentation of Paget's disease includes itching, redness, thickened skin, and ulceration of the nipple, often accompanied by a yellowish or bloody discharge. The lesion typically appears as a sharply demarcated, eczematous plaque that may extend to the areola and surrounding skin. Advanced cases may present with more pronounced changes, such as crusting, scaling, or nipple inversion. Due to its resemblance to other dermatological conditions like eczema, psoriasis, or atopic dermatitis, the diagnosis of Paget's disease is often delayed or misdiagnosed. Genetic mutations, including BRCA1 and BRCA2, are also associated with an increased risk, particularly in males with Klinefelter's syndrome. Endocrine-related conditions, such as obesity or hyperestrogenism, may further contribute to the development of the disease. The prognosis of Paget's disease is primarily determined by the characteristics of the underlying breast carcinoma. Patients with palpable breast tumors, lymph node involvement, or younger age at diagnosis tend to have a worse prognosis. Survival rates are generally lower in males compared to females, likely due to the smaller size of male breast tissue, which may allow for earlier spread of the disease. The mean survival time is approximately 80 months for males and 108 months for females, with five-year survival rates ranging from 20–30% in males and 30–40% in females. Diagnosis of Paget's disease requires a full-thickness biopsy of the nipple and areola to confirm the presence of Paget cells. Imaging studies, including mammography, ultrasonography, and MRI, are used to detect associated breast cancer. While mammography is commonly performed, it has limited sensitivity in detecting DCIS in patients with Paget's disease. MRI is particularly useful in cases where mammography and ultrasonography are inconclusive, as well as for preoperative planning. Treatment for Paget's disease typically involves surgery, with mastectomy being the standard approach. In patients without a palpable lump, the nipple and areola are removed, followed by whole-breast radiation therapy. For those with associated DCIS or invasive breast cancer, complete resection of the underlying malignancy, along with excision of the nipple-areola complex and radiation therapy, is recommended. When lymph nodes are involved, more extensive axillary lymph node surgery may be necessary. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are used as adjuvant or palliative treatments in cases with invasive disease. In summary, Paget's disease of the breast is a rare but significant condition that requires a high index of suspicion for timely diagnosis and management. Its strong association with underlying breast cancer underscores the importance of thorough evaluation and appropriate treatment to improve patient outcomes.
